runs.text: A big problem becomes easy when it is split into small problems, each one with its own name.
The problem
The teacher has the three marks of each of her
4 pupils
. She wants a report card with each pupil's
average
, whether they
passed
(an average of 6 or more) and who had the
best average
How do you organise a program like that without getting lost?
Try it
Work out the report card by hand with these marks: Ana 8, 9 and 10; Beto 5, 6 and 4; Caro 6, 6 and 6; Dani 7, 8 and 6.
The averages are 9, 5, 6 and 7. Ana, Caro and Dani pass; Caro right on the edge, with 6. The best average is Ana's.
Look at how you did it: you did not think about the report card all at once. First you averaged, then you decided who passed and finally you looked for the best.
A new paradigm
Until now you wrote programs as a single list of orders.
Procedural programming
builds a program from smaller pieces, each one with a name and a job, that ask one another for help.

question.text: what if a big program were built from small pieces, each one with a name and a job?

metaphor.text: . It stops working at one point: a piece of program receives different data each time it is used.

history.text: in 1949, on the EDSAC computer in Cambridge, David Wheeler devised how to jump to a piece of program and come back, the basis of subprograms. In 1960, ALGOL 60 formalised them with parameters.

cost.text: you have to decide where to cut and which data to pass to each piece.

entries.text: What goes in and what comes out?
The name and three marks of each pupil go in; one line per pupil and the best average come out.
The average is the money box of
; the best is the best so far of
Which parts does it split into?
Four jobs that can be thought about separately.

runs.text: Splitting a problem into subproblems is a
decomposition
. Drawn from the general to the particular, it is a
decomposition tree

Each job is so small that you already know how to solve it.

runs.text: What you learned

points.text: Procedural programming builds a program from subprograms that call one another.
Decomposing is splitting a problem into subproblems; the decomposition tree draws them from the general to the particular.
A subprogram is a piece of program with a name; calling it is asking it to run.
The parameters are the data it receives; the return value is what it gives back.
